objectives: Classify the major bradyarrhythmias and tachyarrhythmias, including AV blocks and atrial fibrillation/flutter.
Explain the reentry mechanism and contrast it with abnormal automaticity and triggered activity.
Describe the EP study, catheter ablation, pacemakers, and ICDs, and the danger of long-QT syndrome.

slides.title: From normal sinus rhythm to the major arrhythmias
slides.body:
An **arrhythmia** is any deviation from the normal **sinus rhythm**, in which the **SA node** fires regularly at 60-100 bpm and each impulse propagates orderly through the AV node and His-Purkinje system. Arrhythmias divide broadly into too-slow (**bradyarrhythmias**) and too-fast (**tachyarrhythmias**), and by origin into **supraventricular** (above the ventricles) versus **ventricular**.

**Bradyarrhythmias** include **sinus bradycardia**, **sick sinus syndrome** (a failing SA node), and the **atrioventricular (AV) blocks**, graded by severity:

- **First-degree AV block**: every impulse conducts but slowly — a fixed prolonged PR interval over 0.20 s.
- **Second-degree, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)**: the PR interval progressively lengthens beat to beat until one P wave fails to conduct, dropping a QRS, then the cycle resets. Usually benign, in the AV node.
- **Second-degree, Mobitz type II**: the PR is constant but P waves intermittently fail to conduct without warning. More dangerous, usually below the AV node in the His-Purkinje system, and prone to progress.
- **Third-degree (complete) AV block**: no atrial impulses reach the ventricles; the atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation), the ventricles driven by a slow escape pacemaker. A pacemaker indication.

**Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias** include **sinus tachycardia**, **atrial fibrillation (AFib)** — a chaotic, disorganized atrial activity producing an irregularly irregular ventricular response and no organized P waves, the most common sustained arrhythmia and a major cause of **stroke** from atrial thrombus — and **atrial flutter**, a more organized atrial reentry circuit (often around the **cavotricuspid isthmus**) producing 'sawtooth' flutter waves at ~300/min with a regular conducted ventricular rate (often 2:1, giving ~150 bpm). **Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT)** includes **AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)** and **AV reentrant tachycardia (AVRT)** using an accessory pathway as in **Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome**, first described by **Louis Wolff, Sir John Parkinson, and Paul Dudley White** in 1930.

**Ventricular tachyarrhythmias** are the most lethal. **Ventricular tachycardia (VT)** is a fast, wide-QRS rhythm originating below the His bundle, which may degenerate into **ventricular fibrillation (VF)** — disorganized quivering of the ventricles that pumps no blood and causes **sudden cardiac arrest** within seconds unless **defibrillated**. **Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)** and **premature atrial contractions (PACs)** are isolated early beats, usually benign in healthy hearts. Recognizing which arrhythmias are benign and which are immediately life-threatening is the central triage skill of cardiac electrophysiology.

slides.title: Mechanisms: reentry, automaticity, and triggered activity
slides.body:
Three mechanisms generate essentially all arrhythmias, and distinguishing them guides therapy.

**1. Reentry** is the most important and the basis of atrial flutter, AVNRT, AVRT, most VT, and atrial fibrillation. Reentry requires a self-sustaining loop of electrical activity that perpetually re-excites tissue. The classic conditions, articulated by **George Ralph Mines** and **Walter Garrey** around 1913-1914, are: (a) two or more pathways with a region of **unidirectional block**, and (b) **slow conduction** somewhere in the circuit such that by the time the impulse comes around the loop, the tissue it re-enters has recovered from its refractory period. Picture a wave entering a fork: one limb is transiently blocked, so the impulse goes down the open limb, then travels retrograde up the blocked limb (now recovered) and re-enters the original path — a circus movement that spins indefinitely. The **wavelength** of reentry is $\lambda = \text{conduction velocity} \times \text{refractory period}$; reentry is favored when the circuit's physical length exceeds the wavelength. This is why both **slowing conduction** (e.g., scar, ischemia) and **shortening refractoriness** promote reentry, and why drugs that prolong refractoriness (Class III antiarrhythmics) or destroying part of the circuit (ablation) can terminate it.

**2. Abnormal automaticity** arises when cells that should be quiet — or pacemaker cells firing inappropriately — spontaneously depolarize. **Enhanced normal automaticity** speeds the SA node (sinus tachycardia from fever or catecholamines). **Abnormal automaticity** occurs when injured, partially depolarized myocardium acquires pacemaker behavior, as in some ischemic ventricular rhythms or **ectopic atrial tachycardia**.

**3. Triggered activity** depends on **afterdepolarizations** — secondary upswings riding on a preceding action potential. **Early afterdepolarizations (EADs)**, occurring during phases 2-3 when the action potential is abnormally prolonged, are the engine of **torsades de pointes** in **long-QT syndrome**. **Delayed afterdepolarizations (DADs)**, occurring in phase 4 from intracellular **calcium overload**, drive **digoxin toxicity** arrhythmias and catecholaminergic polymorphic VT.

These mechanisms map onto the **Vaughan Williams classification** of antiarrhythmic drugs (proposed by **Miles Vaughan Williams** in 1970): **Class I** sodium-channel blockers (Ia quinidine, Ib lidocaine, Ic flecainide) slow phase-0 conduction; **Class II** beta-blockers blunt sympathetic automaticity; **Class III** potassium-channel blockers (amiodarone, sotalol) prolong refractoriness to interrupt reentry; **Class IV** calcium-channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) slow the AV node. Adenosine, transiently blocking the AV node, terminates AVNRT/AVRT by breaking the reentry loop. Understanding mechanism — reentry versus automaticity versus triggered activity — is what lets the electrophysiologist choose between a drug, an ablation, or a device.

slides.title: The EP study, ablation, and cardiac devices
slides.body:
When the ECG alone cannot localize an arrhythmia, the **electrophysiology (EP) study** maps it directly. Catheters with electrodes are threaded through the femoral veins into the heart, recording **intracardiac electrograms** and pacing the heart to provoke and characterize the arrhythmia. The EP study can pinpoint the site of an accessory pathway, the slow pathway of AVNRT, the isthmus of atrial flutter, or the exit site of a VT circuit. Modern **3D electroanatomic mapping** systems (such as CARTO and EnSite) reconstruct the chamber geometry and color-code activation timing or voltage to find scar.

**Catheter ablation** then destroys the culprit tissue. **Radiofrequency ablation** delivers heat to create a small, controlled lesion; **cryoablation** freezes tissue instead. For **atrial fibrillation**, **pulmonary vein isolation** — encircling the pulmonary veins, the dominant source of triggering ectopy as shown by **Michel Haissaguerre** and colleagues in 1998 — is the cornerstone procedure; newer **pulsed-field ablation** uses electroporation to target myocardium selectively. Ablation can be curative for AVNRT, AVRT (eliminating the accessory pathway), typical atrial flutter, and many VTs, with high success rates.

When the problem is too slow a rhythm or the risk of sudden death, **implantable cardiac devices** intervene:

- A **pacemaker** treats bradyarrhythmias and high-grade AV block by pacing the atrium, ventricle, or both. **Single-chamber** devices pace one chamber; **dual-chamber** devices pace and sense both atrium and ventricle to preserve AV synchrony. The first fully implantable pacemaker was placed in **Arne Larsson** by surgeon **Ake Senning** and engineer **Rune Elmqvist** in 1958.
- An **implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD)**, pioneered by **Michel Mirowski** in 1980, continuously monitors for VT/VF and delivers **antitachycardia pacing** or a **defibrillation shock** to abort sudden cardiac death. ICDs are placed for both **secondary prevention** (survivors of cardiac arrest) and **primary prevention** (e.g., severe HFrEF with EF below 35%).
- **Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT)**, or biventricular pacing, adds a left-ventricular lead to re-coordinate contraction in heart-failure patients with a wide QRS (typically left bundle-branch block), improving ejection fraction and symptoms.
- **Leadless pacemakers** (such as the Micra) and the **subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD)** avoid transvenous leads, reducing infection and lead-failure risk.

Finally, **long-QT syndrome (LQTS)** deserves emphasis as a channelopathy in which delayed repolarization (congenital, from mutations in genes such as **KCNQ1** for LQT1, **KCNH2/hERG** for LQT2, and **SCN5A** for LQT3, or acquired from QT-prolonging drugs and hypokalemia) predisposes to **torsades de pointes**. Management ranges from beta-blockers and avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs to ICDs in high-risk patients. Together, the EP study, ablation, and devices have transformed once-fatal arrhythmias into treatable, often curable, conditions.

question.question: In second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach), what is the characteristic pattern?
options: A fixed prolonged PR interval with every beat conducting
Progressive lengthening of the PR interval until a beat is dropped, then the cycle resets
A constant PR interval with sudden intermittent dropped beats
Complete dissociation of P waves from QRS complexes
question.explanation: Wenckebach (Mobitz I) shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave fails to conduct and a QRS is dropped, after which the sequence restarts. A fixed long PR is first-degree block; a constant PR with sudden drops is Mobitz II; complete P-QRS dissociation is third-degree (complete) block.

hints: The key word is 'progressive' lengthening before the drop.
Contrast it with Mobitz II, where the PR stays constant.
slides.workedSolution: Mobitz I (Wenckebach): PR lengthens progressively, then a QRS drops, then resets — typically a benign AV-nodal phenomenon, unlike the more dangerous infranodal Mobitz II.

question.question: Reentry, the mechanism behind atrial flutter and most VT, classically requires which two conditions?
options: A region of unidirectional block plus slow conduction in the circuit
Early afterdepolarizations and a prolonged QT interval
Vagal stimulation and a short refractory period only
question.explanation: Reentry requires (1) a region of unidirectional block so the impulse travels one way around a loop, and (2) slow conduction so that returning tissue has recovered from refractoriness before the wave re-enters. Automaticity and afterdepolarizations are separate arrhythmia mechanisms, not the requirements for reentry.

hints: Think about why the circulating impulse does not just collide with itself and stop.
One requirement makes the impulse go one direction; the other gives tissue time to recover.
slides.workedSolution: Reentry needs unidirectional block plus slow conduction so the wavelength (velocity x refractory period) fits within the circuit. This is why ablation (cutting the circuit) and Class III drugs (prolonging refractoriness) terminate reentrant arrhythmias.

question.question: In typical atrial flutter the atrial rate is about 300 beats per minute. If the AV node conducts every second flutter wave (2:1 conduction), what is the resulting ventricular rate in beats per minute?
question.hint: With 2:1 conduction, only half the atrial impulses reach the ventricles, so divide the atrial rate by 2.

question.question: A young athlete with sudden palpitations and a delta wave
question.prompt: A 19-year-old collegiate athlete has recurrent episodes of a sudden, regular, fast heartbeat. Between episodes his baseline ECG shows a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS called a delta wave. Identify the underlying syndrome and the anatomical abnormality responsible (an accessory pathway), explain how this pathway enables an AV reentrant tachycardia, and describe why catheter ablation of the accessory pathway can be curative. Why is this condition relevant to sudden cardiac death risk, particularly if the patient develops atrial fibrillation?

question.question: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), pioneered by Michel Mirowski, is most appropriate for which purpose?
options: Pacing the atrium in symptomatic sinus bradycardia
Re-coordinating contraction in left bundle-branch block
Detecting ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation and delivering a shock to prevent sudden death
Curing atrial fibrillation by isolating the pulmonary veins
question.explanation: An ICD continuously monitors for VT/VF and delivers antitachycardia pacing or a defibrillation shock to abort sudden cardiac death, used for primary prevention (e.g., EF below 35%) and secondary prevention (arrest survivors). Bradycardia is treated by a pacemaker, dyssynchrony by CRT, and AFib by pulmonary vein isolation/ablation.

hints: The device's defining action is delivering a shock for a lethal fast rhythm.
Distinguish it from a pacemaker (too-slow rhythms) and CRT (dyssynchrony).
slides.workedSolution: The ICD detects VT/VF and shocks to prevent sudden cardiac death (Mirowski, 1980). Pacemakers treat bradycardia, CRT treats dyssynchrony from wide QRS, and ablation treats reentrant/triggered tachycardias like AFib.
